citation.title: Sharp Bounds for Complier Average Potential Outcomes in Experiments with Noncompliance and Incomplete Reporting

standing_assumptions: The work is a three-page letter (Statistics and Probability Letters 83 (2013) 677–679) with one proposition and one corollary, each with a short printed proof, and one application. Everything below was read from the rendered page images (the staged pages, and the staged PDF re-rendered at 260 dpi when this list was fixed). [Setting: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “We follow the setup of Angrist and Pischke (2009, Chapter 4). Let $Y_i(d, z)$ be the potential outcome of unit $i$ under treatment $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$, let $D_i(z)$ be the potential treatment of unit $i$ under assignment $z$, and let $Z_i$ be the treatment assigned to unit $i$. The causal effect for unit $i$ is then $Y_i(1, Z_i) - Y_i(0, Z_i)$. We assume (i) random assignment: $[Y_i(d, z), D_i(z) : d, z \in \{0, 1\}] \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; (ii) exclusion restriction: $Y_i(d, z)$ does not depend on $z$, so we may write $Y_i(d, z) = Y_i(d)$; (iii) non-zero first-stage effect: $E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)] \ne 0$; (iv) monotonicity: $\forall i$, $D_i(1) \ge D_i(0)$. We make two notational simplifications. First, given (i), labels are exchangeable and so we drop notational dependence on $i$. Second, we define $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, and $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$.” [LATE display and bounded outcomes: Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “This setting implies that the ``LATE theorem'' (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) holds: the CACE, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]}{\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]} = \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},$$ where each component may be estimated using sample analogues to population quantities. The associated estimator is logically equivalent to the Wald instrumental variables estimator (Angrist et al., 1996). We make one additional assumption to ensure partial identification: we require that outcomes are bounded. Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$.” [Typography] The page prints the expectation operator upright in most places ($\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$) and in italics in assumption (iii) ($E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)]$); it is one operator. $EY_1$, $EY_0$, $EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$ and $P_c$ are names of real numbers, not products. [What the paper does not print] The paper does not define the observed treatment $D$ and the observed outcome $Y$ that appear in $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z]$, $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = z]$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$ (the relations $D = D(Z)$ and $Y = Y(D(Z))$ are not displayed). It does not say that both assignment arms have positive probability. It does not assume $P_c < 1$: (iii) and (iv) give $0 < P_c \le 1$ only, and ‘two-sided noncompliance’ is stated in Section 4 for the application alone. It does not say whether ‘$Y \in [0, 1]$’ bounds the observed outcome or both potential outcomes. It does not define ‘known’, ‘sharp’, ‘identified’ or ‘point identified’. It has no response or missing-data indicator and no assumption about outcomes that are not recorded. [Remarks for the formalizer, not printed in the paper] The reading the audit's validators settled on is: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$. The unit index is suppressed as generic-unit population notation; the validator of finding P028-N002 (rated a clarity note) established that the printed reason for dropping it (‘given (i), labels are exchangeable’) does not follow from (i) and is not needed, and that no identical-distribution or random-sampling assumption has to be added. Principal strata: compliers $C = \{D(1) > D(0)\} = \{D(0) = 0, D(1) = 1\}$, always-takers $A = \{D(0) = D(1) = 1\}$, never-takers $N = \{D(0) = D(1) = 0\}$; monotonicity excludes $\{D(0) = 1, D(1) = 0\}$, so $D(1) - D(0) = \mathbf{1}_C$, $P_c = \Pr(C) = \mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]$ and $0 < P_c \le 1$; $\Pr(A) = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$, $\Pr(N) = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$ and $\Pr(A) + \Pr(N) = 1 - P_c$. A conditional mean given an event is the elementary one and is defined only when the event has positive probability. Lean's division is total ($x/0 = 0$), so a statement that a printed quotient or conditional mean is undefined has to be stated as the failure of a side condition (a zero denominator, a null conditioning event), not as a property of the quotient's value. Boundedness is used only in Proposition 1; the LATE display and Corollary 1 need integrable outcomes only. [Why the list has ten targets] Three findings rated as errors concern a mathematical statement or rest on an exact formal counterexample. P028-N005 (Moderate): the application presents point estimates of the complier means although 71 of 1000 outcomes are missing and no response assumption is stated; the validator confirmed this with two exact laws that agree on everything observed and disagree on the complier means, so the counterexample (T1), the formal content of the corrected claim (T2) and the passage as printed (T3) are targets. P028-E001 (Minor): a misprinted upper limit and a wrong symbol in the proof of Proposition 1; corrected statement (T4) and the validator's counterexample to the printed intermediate system (T5). P028-E002 (Minor): the proof of Proposition 1 does not cover $P_c = 1$; corrected statement (T6) and the validator's counterexample to the unqualified proof step (T7). The fourth error, P028-E003 (Minor), is a volume number in the reference list and has no mathematical statement to correct. P028-N002 and P028-N007 are clarity notes; P028-N003, P028-N004 and P028-N006 were not confirmed; P028-N001 is undetermined. Of the seven headline claims, H1 (Proposition 1, T8), H3 (Corollary 1, T9) and H2 (the LATE identity and the statement that the three figures do not identify the complier means, T10) are mathematical statements. H4 (the count of 6 of 20 studies), H5 and H6 (the application's estimates) and H7 (the reporting recommendation) are an empirical count, empirical estimates and a recommendation, and are not targets; the formal content behind H6 is reached through P028-N005.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4, second paragraph: ‘we are able to fill in the necessary missing information ... Application of Corollary 1 yields ...’, read as the claim that the replication data and the assumptions of Section 2 point identify the complier average potential outcomes; the two witnesses are the validator's constructions and are not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 679 (PDF p. 3), Section 4, second paragraph; the assumptions are on p. 678 (PDF p. 2), Section 2
canonical_claim.statement:
Two exact witnesses (validator's constructions; not in the paper): two probability laws that satisfy every assumption of Section 2 with binary outcomes, give the same law of everything that is observed when the outcome is recorded for some units only, and have different complier average potential outcomes.
Notation for both witnesses. $Z \in \{0,1\}$ is assignment, with $\Pr[Z = 0] = 99/200$ and $\Pr[Z = 1] = 101/200$. $S \in \{A, N, C\}$ is the principal stratum, with $(D(0), D(1)) = (1,1)$ on $A$ (always-takers), $(0,0)$ on $N$ (never-takers) and $(0,1)$ on $C$ (compliers), and $$\Pr[S = A] = p_a = \tfrac{16}{99}, \qquad \Pr[S = N] = p_n = \tfrac{64}{101}, \qquad \Pr[S = C] = p_c = \tfrac{2047}{9999}.$$ $Y(0), Y(1) \in \{0,1\}$ are the potential outcomes ($Y(d,z) = Y(d)$). $R(0), R(1) \in \{0,1\}$ are potential response indicators: $R(z) = 1$ when the outcome is recorded under assignment $z$. $Z$ is independent of $(S, Y(0), Y(1), R(0), R(1))$. Observed variables: $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D)$, $R = R(Z)$; the outcome is seen only when $R = 1$, so the observed data are $(Z, D, R, R \cdot Y)$.
Source table. For the cell $(Z = z, D = d)$ let $s_{zd1}$, $s_{zd0}$, $m_{zd}$ be the numbers of recorded ones, recorded zeros and missing outcomes, and let $n_0 = 495$, $n_1 = 505$: cell $(0,0)$: $167,\ 212,\ 36$; cell $(0,1)$: $40,\ 39,\ 1$; cell $(1,0)$: $130,\ 164,\ 26$; cell $(1,1)$: $110,\ 67,\ 8$. (So $415 + 80 = 495$, $320 + 185 = 505$, and 71 of 1000 outcomes are missing.)
Construction. A witness is fixed by a completion $x = (x_{00}, x_{01}, x_{10}, x_{11})$ with integers $0 \le x_{zd} \le m_{zd}$ ($x_{zd}$ is the number of missing outcomes of cell $(z,d)$ that are ones). Put $t_{zd1} = s_{zd1} + x_{zd}$, $t_{zd0} = s_{zd0} + m_{zd} - x_{zd}$, $a = t_{011}/80$, $b = t_{101}/320$ and $$\mu_0 = \frac{t_{001}/495 - t_{101}/505}{p_c}, \qquad \mu_1 = \frac{t_{111}/505 - t_{011}/495}{p_c}.$$ Given $S = A$: $Y(0) = 0$ and $Y(1) \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(a)$. Given $S = N$: $Y(0) \sim \mathrm{Bernoulli}(b)$ and $Y(1) = 0$. Given $S = C$: $Y(0)$ and $Y(1)$ are independent Bernoulli variables with means $\mu_0$ and $\mu_1$. Given $S$ and $(Y(0), Y(1))$: $R(0)$ and $R(1)$ are independent Bernoulli variables with success probabilities $q_{0,\,D(0),\,Y(D(0))}$ and $q_{1,\,D(1),\,Y(D(1))}$, where $q_{zdv} = s_{zdv}/t_{zdv}$.
Lower witness: $x = (0, 1, 26, 0)$, so $a = 41/80$, $b = 39/80$, $\mu_0 = 1423/10235$, $\mu_1 = 6749/10235$. Upper witness: $x = (36, 0, 0, 8)$, so $a = 1/2$, $b = 13/32$, $\mu_0 = 7633/10235$, $\mu_1 = 7642/10235$. Each witness is a law with 17 atoms of positive rational mass on $(S, Y(0), Y(1), R(0), R(1))$, times the law of $Z$; the atoms and their masses are listed in the validator's models.json.
Claims. (N1) In each witness the masses are positive and sum to 1; $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1), R(0), R(1))$ is independent of $Z$; $D(1) \ge D(0)$ on every atom; $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = P_c = 2047/9999 \ne 0$; $Y(0), Y(1) \in \{0,1\} \subset [0,1]$; $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$. So assumptions (i)–(iv) of Section 2 and bounded outcomes hold, and random assignment holds for the response potentials as well.
(N2) In both witnesses, for all $z, d, v \in \{0,1\}$, $$\Pr[D = d, R = 1, Y = v \mid Z = z] = \frac{s_{zdv}}{n_z}, \qquad \Pr[D = d, R = 0 \mid Z = z] = \frac{m_{zd}}{n_z}.$$ Hence the two witnesses have the same law of the observed data $(Z, D, R, R \cdot Y)$. In particular both have $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] = 16/99$, $\Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 64/101$, respondent arm means $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0, R = 1] = 207/458$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1, R = 1] = 240/471$, and respondent cell means $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0, R = 1] = 40/79$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1, R = 1] = 130/294$.
(N3) $\bigl(\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)],\ \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]\bigr)$ equals $(1423/10235,\ 6749/10235)$ in the lower witness and $(7633/10235,\ 7642/10235)$ in the upper witness. The two pairs differ in both coordinates.
(N4) The full-population arm means differ between the witnesses: $(EY_0, EY_1) = (208/495,\ 266/505)$ in the lower and $(27/55,\ 248/505)$ in the upper; in each witness the formula of Corollary 1 evaluated at the witness's own full-population moments returns the pair in (N3).
(N5) The formula of Corollary 1 evaluated at the respondent moments of (N2), with the take-up probabilities of all units, gives the same pair in both witnesses, $$\left(\frac{1594452863}{3629163146},\ \frac{896530960}{1244058109}\right) \approx (0.4393,\ 0.7207),$$ which is the pair of complier means of neither witness.
Consequence. The law of the observed data $(Z, D, R, R \cdot Y)$ together with assumptions (i)–(iv) and bounded outcomes does not determine $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ or $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$: there is no function of the observed law that equals either complier mean in every model satisfying the assumptions. The printed inference from the replication data to the two point values therefore needs an added condition on response (P028-T2).

The complier average potential outcomes $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$ and the formula of Corollary 1: p. 678, transcribed in P028-T9. In the application $Z$ is the encouragement to watch a mayoral debate, $D$ is watching and $Y$ is ‘changed views about at least one candidate’ (p. 679).
Not in the paper; defined by the validator (derivation.md, sections ‘Source reconstruction’, ‘Exact completions and the Corollary 1 identity’ and ‘Explicit compatible potential-outcome and response laws’): the response indicators $R(z)$ and $R$; the source table, which is the cross-tabulation of the staged replication data of Mullainathan et al. (2010) with $Z$ the stored assignment variable, $D$ the stored binary viewing variable (held fixed) and $Y$ built as in the source study's script (1 if either candidate opinion changed, 0 if both are unchanged, missing otherwise); the completions $x$; the stratum masses $p_a = 80/495$, $p_n = 320/505$, $p_c = 1 - p_a - p_n$; $a = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|A]$, $b = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|N]$, $\mu_d = \mathrm{E}[Y(d)|C]$; the response probabilities $q_{zdv}$. The validator reads the empirical conditional arm tables as a possible exact population law: ‘This is a legitimate superpopulation counterexample; it is not a claim that empirical proportions equal the actual experiment's unknown population probabilities.’
canonical_claim.note: P028-N005 is rated an error, Moderate (ratings.json), so this target and P028-T2 have priority 2. The finding concerns the application, not Corollary 1; it is a target because it rests on this exact non-identification argument and its repair is a missing assumption. Sol's verdict is confirmed_in_part with evidence type exact_counterexample: what is established is an omitted response condition and an unqualified inference in Section 4; what is not established is any bias, its sign or size, or that 0.43 or 0.72 is numerically wrong (the three plug-in conventions the validator computed give 0.436 to 0.439 for the control mean and 0.712 to 0.721 for the treated mean). The re-run (validate/P028-N005/recheck-v1/recheck.json) upheld the verdict with no corrections and checked the 17 atoms of each law independently. When this list was fixed the construction above was rebuilt from the source table in exact rational arithmetic: it reproduces every atom and mass of both laws in validate/P028-N005/v1/artifact/models.json, both laws have total mass 1, their observed laws coincide with the source table, and (N3)–(N5) hold as stated. The witnesses are the two extreme completions; the validator also built a compatible law at each of the 16 corner completions. For a Lean statement only the conditional laws given $Z$ matter, and the 17 atoms can be taken from models.json; a statement that asserts (N2) and (N3) for two explicit finite laws satisfying (N1) is the target. The choice $Y(0) = 0$ on $A$ and $Y(1) = 0$ on $N$ fixes potential outcomes that are never observed and is immaterial. The stored viewing variable codes three control respondents who answered ‘not sure/refused’ as non-viewers, which is why $p_a = 80/495$ here while the paper prints $0.163 = 80/492$; this does not affect the argument, which is about exact laws and not about the experiment. The CACE also differs between the witnesses ($5326/10235$ and $9/10235$), because the full-population arm means differ; the finding as rated concerns the point estimates of the second paragraph, and the ratings record H5 as also touched.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4, second paragraph, the inference from the replication data to the complier means 0.43 and 0.72, as repaired by Sol: identification of the complier average potential outcomes from incompletely recorded outcomes under a stated response condition
canonical_claim.location: p. 679 (PDF p. 3), Section 4, second paragraph; Corollary 1 is on p. 678 (PDF p. 2)
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P028-N005, smallest_repair), verbatim: "State the target population, outcome/viewing coding and analysis denominators, and qualify the application by a sufficient response assumption for the moments actually estimated. For the mixed available-case approach, mean equality between respondents and the full population is needed for both assignment-arm outcome means and the two noncomplier-cell outcome means; response independent of (Y,D) within each assignment arm is one sufficient stronger condition. If assuming only mean-ignorable response within (D,Z) cells, reweight the observed cell means by full-sample cell probabilities before applying Corollary 1 and recompute. Without an added response assumption, replace the point-identification inference with missing-outcome sensitivity bounds."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections ‘Exact completions and the Corollary 1 identity’ and ‘Repair and dependency’). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$; in addition a response indicator $R \in \{0,1\}$ on the same space (the outcome is recorded when $R = 1$; $Z$ and $D$ are recorded for every unit). Write $C = \{D(1) > D(0)\}$, $P_c = \Pr(C) = \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0] > 0$, $c_d = \mathrm{E}[Y(d)|C]$, $q = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$, $r = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$, so that $P_c = 1 - q - r$.
(i) [Corollary 1 in joint-moment form; no condition on $R$ and no positivity of cells.] $$P_c\, c_0 = \mathrm{E}[Y(1 - D)|Z = 0] - \mathrm{E}[Y(1 - D)|Z = 1], \qquad P_c\, c_1 = \mathrm{E}[Y D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y D|Z = 0].$$
(ii) [Mixed available-case version: take-up from all units, outcome means from respondents.] Suppose $q > 0$, $r > 0$, $\Pr[R = 1|Z = z] > 0$ for $z = 0, 1$, $\Pr[R = 1|D = 1, Z = 0] > 0$, $\Pr[R = 1|D = 0, Z = 1] > 0$, and (M1) $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z, R = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z]$ for $z = 0, 1$; (M2) $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0, R = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1, R = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$. Then $$c_0 = \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0, R = 1] - q\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0, R = 1] - r\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1, R = 1]}{P_c}, \qquad c_1 = c_0 + \frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1, R = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0, R = 1]}{P_c}.$$
(iii) [A sufficient stronger condition.] If, for each $z \in \{0,1\}$, $R$ is independent of $(Y, D)$ conditionally on $Z = z$ and $\Pr[R = 1|Z = z] > 0$, then (M1) holds, (M2) holds whenever $q > 0$ and $r > 0$, and the response probabilities required in (ii) are positive; so the conclusion of (ii) holds.
(iv) [Mean-ignorable response within $(D, Z)$ cells.] Suppose that for every $(d, z)$ with $\Pr[D = d|Z = z] > 0$, $\Pr[R = 1|D = d, Z = z] > 0$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z, R = 1] = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$. Then, with the term of an empty cell omitted in each expression, $EY_z = \sum_{d} \Pr[D = d|Z = z]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z, R = 1]$ for $z = 0, 1$ and $$c_0 = \frac{\Pr[D = 0|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 0, R = 1] - r\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1, R = 1]}{P_c}, \qquad c_1 = \frac{\Pr[D = 1|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 1, R = 1] - q\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0, R = 1]}{P_c}.$$ Under this hypothesis alone the unweighted respondent arm means $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = z, R = 1]$ need not equal $EY_z$, so the formula of (ii) is not justified by it.
(v) [No response condition: sensitivity bounds.] With no condition on $R$, $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[R Y (1 - D)|Z = 0] - \mathrm{E}[R Y (1 - D)|Z = 1] - \Pr[R = 0, D = 0|Z = 1]}{P_c} \ \le\ c_0\ \le\ \frac{\mathrm{E}[R Y (1 - D)|Z = 0] + \Pr[R = 0, D = 0|Z = 0] - \mathrm{E}[R Y (1 - D)|Z = 1]}{P_c},$$ $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[R Y D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[R Y D|Z = 0] - \Pr[R = 0, D = 1|Z = 0]}{P_c} \ \le\ c_1\ \le\ \frac{\mathrm{E}[R Y D|Z = 1] + \Pr[R = 0, D = 1|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[R Y D|Z = 0]}{P_c},$$ and every quantity on the outer sides is a function of the law of the observed data $(Z, D, R, R \cdot Y)$.
Worked instance (the source table of P028-T1, read as a population law; validator's output.txt). (ii) gives $\left(\tfrac{1594452863}{3629163146}, \tfrac{896530960}{1244058109}\right) \approx (0.4393, 0.7207)$; (iv) gives $\left(\tfrac{16568969}{38014837}, \tfrac{295510}{414829}\right) \approx (0.4359, 0.7124)$; (v) gives $c_0 \in \left[\tfrac{1423}{10235}, \tfrac{7633}{10235}\right] \approx [0.1390, 0.7458]$ and $c_1 \in \left[\tfrac{6749}{10235}, \tfrac{7642}{10235}\right] \approx [0.6594, 0.7467]$, and each of the four endpoints is attained by a witness of P028-T1, so for this observed law the bounds of (v) cannot be narrowed without a response condition.

From the paper. Assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$: Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2), standing assumptions. Corollary 1 and its formula: p. 678, transcribed in P028-T9. The passage being repaired: Section 4, second paragraph, p. 679 (PDF p. 3), transcribed in P028-T3. ‘Sample analogues to population quantities’: Section 2, p. 678 (the paper's only statement of how the population moments are estimated).
Not in the paper; defined by the validator: the response indicator $R$ ($R = 1$ when the outcome constructed by the source study is recorded); the ‘mixed available-case approach’ (take-up probabilities from all records, outcome means from records with a recorded outcome); the mean equalities (M1) and (M2), which are the displayed equalities of derivation.md, section ‘Repair and dependency’; the cell-reweighting formula for $EY_z$ in (iv), displayed in the same section. $R \cdot Y$ is the recorded outcome, taken as 0 when $R = 0$; $\mathrm{E}[R Y (1 - D)|Z = z]$ and $\mathrm{E}[R Y D|Z = z]$ are product moments within an assignment arm and need no positivity of $(D, Z)$ cells.
canonical_claim.note: Repair as settled in validated.json (sol.smallest_repair; the candidate carried no prior correction). Repair cost recorded by Sol: new_assumption_applications_may_not_satisfy; a response condition is not supplied by randomization and is not verified in the paper, and the only repair with no new assumption weakens the conclusion to the bounds of (v). (i) is the validator's rewriting of Corollary 1 ‘with joint outcome masses’ and is the product-moment form of P028-T6 (v); (ii) and (iv) follow from Corollary 1 (P028-T9) by substituting the assumed equalities; (iii) is elementary. Sol states (M1) and (M2) as needed for the mixed approach and (iii) as ‘one sufficient stronger condition’; the target is sufficiency, as written. The two-sided inequalities of (v) are this list's statement, in population notation and for outcomes in $[0,1]$, of the validator's completion range: the validator derives $p_c\mu_0 = (167 + x_{00})/495 - (130 + x_{10})/505$ and $p_c\mu_1 = (110 + x_{11})/505 - (40 + x_{01})/495$ for binary outcomes and takes the extremes over $0 \le x_{zd} \le m_{zd}$; the general form follows from (i) and $0 \le \mathrm{E}[(1 - R)\,Y\,\mathbf{1}\{D = d\}|Z = z] \le \Pr[R = 0, D = d|Z = z]$. It was written out, and the worked instance recomputed in exact rational arithmetic, when this list was fixed; the numerical values agree with the validator's output.txt and with the re-run's independent check. Neither witness of P028-T1 satisfies (M1) (the full arm mean $EY_0$ is $208/495$ in one and $27/55$ in the other, against the respondent mean $207/458$) or the hypothesis of (iv). What this target does not assert: that any of these response conditions holds in the experiment, which convention the authors used (their script is not available), or that the completion ranges are sampling intervals. A common complete-case analysis is not a repair by itself: selecting on a response indicator that may depend on assignment does not automatically preserve random assignment among the selected units (validator's derivation).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Section 4 (Application), second paragraph, as printed, with the sentence of Section 2 on estimation by sample analogues
canonical_claim.location: p. 679 (PDF p. 3), Section 4, second paragraph, with footnote 2; p. 678 (PDF p. 2), Section 2, second paragraph
canonical_claim.statement:
As printed. Section 4, second paragraph, p. 679 (PDF p. 3): “Point identification is possible when additional information about the joint distribution of $Y$, $D$, $Z$ is known. Since the replication data set is publicly available for the study$^2$, we are able to fill in the necessary missing information: $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] = 0.163$, $\Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 0.634$, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] = 0.506$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1] = 0.442$. Application of Corollary 1 yields $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = 0.43$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = 0.72$. Our inferences are considerably tightened by knowledge of additional features of the distribution that were not reported.”
Footnote 2, p. 679: “The replication data set for Mullainathan et al. (2010) is archived at http://isps.research.yale.edu/data/D049/.”
The paragraph that precedes it, Section 4, first paragraph, p. 679: “We consider the encouragement study reported by Mullainathan et al. (2010), which randomly assigned an encouragement to watch a mayoral debate ($Z$) in order to assess the effect of watching ($D$) on changed views about at least one candidate ($Y$). The experiment had two-sided noncompliance, as both $\Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] > 0$ and $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] > 0$. The authors report estimates of $EY_0 = 0.45$, $EY_1 = 0.51$ and $P_c = 0.21$. While the CACE can be estimated as 29 percentage points, the authors do not provide sufficient information for point estimation of complier average potential outcomes. We now estimate sharp bounds on complier potential outcomes by application of Proposition 1. The bounds are rather wide: $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] \in [0, 0.71]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] \in [0.29, 1]$. Thus, although the CACE is identified, very little information is conveyed on complier potential outcomes by the published results.”
The paper's statement on estimation, Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2), after the LATE display: “where each component may be estimated using sample analogues to population quantities.”
The hypotheses the paper attaches are those of Section 2 (assumptions (i)–(iv) and bounded outcomes, transcribed in the standing assumptions) and Corollary 1 (P028-T9). No response indicator, analysis population or assumption about unrecorded outcomes is printed anywhere in the paper.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: $Z$, $D$, $Y$ in the application: Section 4, first paragraph, p. 679: an encouragement to watch a mayoral debate ($Z$), watching ($D$), changed views about at least one candidate ($Y$). $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$, $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$, $P_c$ and the formula applied: Corollary 1 and Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2), transcribed in P028-T9 and the standing assumptions. The four ‘filled in’ quantities are the two off-diagonal take-up probabilities and the two off-diagonal cell means that enter Corollary 1; the paper does not say from which respondents each is computed. Not in the paper: the staged replication data have 1000 respondents, of whom 71 have no recorded outcome under the source study's construction (37 of 495 controls, 34 of 505 encouraged), with 36, 1, 26 and 8 missing in the cells $(Z,D) = (0,0), (0,1), (1,0), (1,1)$ (validator's derivation.md, section ‘Source reconstruction’).
canonical_claim.note: Not a mathematical statement in the paper: an application passage, listed because finding P028-N005 is rated Moderate and the brief asks for the statement as printed. Its first sentence is a correct conditional statement (the full joint law of $(Y, D, Z)$ identifies the complier means; that is Corollary 1, P028-T9) and is not what the finding concerns. The formalizable content of the rest, on the validator's natural reading (‘the available replication information suffices for point estimation under the standing causal assumptions’), is the universal claim that, when outcomes are recorded for some units only, every law satisfying the assumptions of Section 2 has complier means equal to the formula of Corollary 1 evaluated at the take-up probabilities of all units and the outcome means of respondents; equivalently, that the law of $(Z, D, R, R \cdot Y)$ and the assumptions determine the complier means. That rendering is this audit's reading, not the paper's wording, and P028-T1 refutes it: (N5) there shows the formula returning one pair for two laws whose complier means are different pairs. If nothing can be stated beyond the universal claim that P028-T1 already refutes, not_applicable is the right status for this target. The printed numbers themselves are not part of the target: 0.43 and 0.72 are estimates, no printed value is shown to be wrong, and the questions about the precision and consistency of the seven printed inputs are finding P028-N007 (a clarity note). The brief's priority scale has no level for a printed statement that is not a mathematical headline result; 3 is used so that it follows the counterexample and the corrected statement, as in earlier works of this audit.

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1, the sentence between Eq. (3) and the three-line display, corrected: upper limit $1 - P_c$ (printed 1) and ‘the implied value of $EY_c(0)$’ (printed $EY_c(1)$)
canonical_claim.statement:
Corrected text (validated.json, P028-E001: smallest_repair and prior_correction.corrected_text). The sentence after Eq. (3) reads: “such that $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, and $0 \le EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) \le 1 - P_c$. Then substituting the implied value of $EY_c(0)$ from Eq. (3) into the system of inequalities and rearranging terms, we obtain” followed by the three displayed lines, which are unchanged: $$0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1,$$ $$(EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le 1 + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c,$$ $$(EY_1 + P_c - 1)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le EY_1/P_c.$$ Sol's repair, verbatim: "Replace $0\le EY_1-P_cEY_c(1)\le1$ by $0\le EY_1-P_cEY_c(1)\le1-P_c$; replace “the implied value of $EY_c(1)$” by “the implied value of $EY_c(0)$”."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis. Let $p, e_0, e_1, x_0, x_1$ be real numbers with $0 < p < 1$ (they stand for $P_c$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$), and put $\tau = (e_1 - e_0)/p$.
(i) [The reframing is an equivalence.] There is a real number $n$ with $$p\,x_0 + (1 - p)\,n = e_0, \qquad p\,x_1 + (1 - p)\,n = e_1, \qquad 0 \le x_0 \le 1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 1,\quad 0 \le n \le 1$$ if and only if $$p\,x_0 + e_1 - p\,x_1 = e_0, \qquad 0 \le x_0 \le 1,\quad 0 \le x_1 \le 1,\quad 0 \le e_1 - p\,x_1 \le 1 - p.$$ When such an $n$ exists it is $n = (e_1 - p\,x_1)/(1 - p)$.
(ii) [Substituting the implied value of $x_0$.] $p\,x_0 + e_1 - p\,x_1 = e_0$ if and only if $x_0 = x_1 - \tau$. If $x_0 = x_1 - \tau$, then $0 \le x_0 \le 1 \iff \tau \le x_1 \le 1 + \tau$. Moreover $0 \le e_1 - p\,x_1 \le 1 - p \iff (e_1 + p - 1)/p \le x_1 \le e_1/p$.
(iii) [The intervals of Proposition 1.] Hence the system of (i) holds if and only if $x_0 = x_1 - \tau$ and $$\max\left\{0,\ \tau,\ 1 - \frac{1 - e_1}{p}\right\} \le x_1 \le \min\left\{1,\ 1 + \tau,\ \frac{e_1}{p}\right\}$$ (note $(e_1 + p - 1)/p = 1 - (1 - e_1)/p$), which is the treated interval of Proposition 1. Subtracting $\tau$ from its endpoints gives the control interval: $$\max\left\{0, \tau, 1 - \frac{1 - e_1}{p}\right\} - \tau = \max\left\{0,\ -\tau,\ 1 - \frac{1 - e_0}{p}\right\}, \qquad \min\left\{1, 1 + \tau, \frac{e_1}{p}\right\} - \tau = \min\left\{1,\ 1 - \tau,\ \frac{e_0}{p}\right\}.$$
(iv) [What the printed constraint gives.] $0 \le e_1 - p\,x_1 \le 1 \iff (e_1 - 1)/p \le x_1 \le e_1/p$. If $e_1 \le 1$, the lower half is implied by $x_1 \ge 0$, so the printed third constraint adds only $x_1 \le e_1/p$ and does not give the lower limit $(e_1 + p - 1)/p$ of the third displayed line; the system with the printed constraint is implied by, and is not equivalent to, the system with $0 \le n \le 1$ (P028-T5).
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: The printed proof, Eqs. (1)–(3), $EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$ and the proposition's two intervals: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), transcribed in P028-T8. $P_c$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$: Section 2, p. 678, standing assumptions. In (i)–(iv) the letters $p, e_0, e_1, x_0, x_1, n$ are real variables and no probability model is needed; $\tau$ is the CACE $(EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c$ of the LATE display. The case $P_c = 1$, where the printed division by $1 - P_c$ is not available, is the subject of P028-T6 and P028-T7.
canonical_claim.note: P028-E001 is rated an error, Minor (ratings.json): two misprints in one sentence of the proof; the author's instruction is that the corrected version of every mathematical error is formalized, so it is a target at priority 3. Sol's verdict is confirmed (batch P028-B01, evidence type complete_derivation; repair cost none): the sentence is false as printed, the intended constraint is clear from the lines before and after it, and the three displayed lines, the proposition, its sharpness and the application bounds are unchanged. The complete derivation is the docstring of the artifact named here, with exact checks in the same file (output: check_math.txt beside it; verdict: validate/_batch/P028-B01/verdicts.json); the prior correction was found correct. (i)–(iii) are that derivation with the two directions of each equivalence written out; (iv) restates what Sol records as established (‘The printed weaker constraint alone gives lower bound $(EY_1-1)/P_c$, rather than the next displayed $(EY_1+P_c-1)/P_c$’). canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1, the system printed after Eq. (3) (‘such that ... and $0 \le EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) \le 1$’), offered as a reframing of Eqs. (1)–(2) with their constraints; the witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), proof of Proposition 1, between Eq. (3) and the three-line display
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness (validator's; not in the paper) that the system printed after Eq. (3) is not equivalent to Eqs. (1)–(2) with the constraints $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_n \le 1$. Take $$P_c = \tfrac12, \qquad EY_0 = EY_1 = \tfrac34, \qquad EY_c(0) = EY_c(1) = 0.$$
Claims. (E1) Eq. (3) holds: $\tfrac12 \cdot 0 + \tfrac34 - \tfrac12 \cdot 0 = \tfrac34$. (E2) The three printed constraints hold: $0 \le EY_c(0) = 0 \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) = 0 \le 1$ and $0 \le EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = \tfrac34 \le 1$. (E3) The value of $EY_n$ given by Eq. (2) is $[EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c) = (3/4)/(1/2) = 3/2 > 1$; so no $EY_n \in [0,1]$ satisfies Eqs. (1)–(2) with these complier means, and the corrected constraint fails: $EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = \tfrac34 > \tfrac12 = 1 - P_c$. (E4) The printed third constraint gives only $EY_c(1) \ge (EY_1 - 1)/P_c = -\tfrac12$, whereas the third displayed line of the proof has $EY_c(1) \ge (EY_1 + P_c - 1)/P_c = \tfrac12$. (E5) For $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac34, \tfrac34)$ the set of values of $EY_c(1)$ admitted by the printed system (Eq. (3) with the three printed constraints) is $[0, 1]$, while the set admitted by Eqs. (1)–(2) with their constraints, which is the treated interval of Proposition 1, is $[\tfrac12, 1]$; since $(EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c = 0$ the same holds for $EY_c(0)$. (E6) The triple is attained under the assumptions of Section 2: a population with a fraction $\tfrac12$ of compliers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = 1$ and a fraction $\tfrac12$ of never-takers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = \tfrac12$, assigned by an independent fair coin, has $P_c = \tfrac12$ and $EY_0 = EY_1 = \tfrac34$.
Consequence. The printed reframing admits complier means that no model with the given $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1)$ has, and the third displayed line of the proof does not follow from the printed third constraint. Proposition 1 itself is not contradicted: its intervals for this triple are $[\tfrac12, 1]$ and $[\tfrac12, 1]$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Eqs. (1)–(3), $EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$, the printed constraints and the three displayed lines: proof of Proposition 1, p. 678 (PDF p. 2), transcribed in P028-T8. $P_c$, $EY_0$, $EY_1$: Section 2, p. 678, standing assumptions. The witness is a point $(p, e_0, e_1, x_0, x_1) = (\tfrac12, \tfrac34, \tfrac34, 0, 0)$ in the notation of P028-T4; (E1)–(E5) are statements about real numbers. (E6) uses the construction by which the validator proves sharpness (compliers with constant outcomes $(x - \tau, x)$ and never-takers with both potential outcomes $(EY_1 - P_c\,x)/(1 - P_c)$, here with $x = 1$).
canonical_claim.note: Counterexample to the printed statement of a Minor error (P028-E001); priority 3, with its corrected statement P028-T4. The witness is the validator's (‘With P_c=1/2, EY_0=EY_1=3/4, EY_c(0)=EY_c(1)=0, the printed system holds but implies EY_n=3/2; the correct interval is [1/2,1], whereas the printed system gives [0,1]’), first given by the Sol fresh reader; the script named here asserts (E1)–(E3) and (E5) in exact arithmetic (output: check_math.txt). (E6) is not asserted by the script for this triple; it is the validator's sharpness construction evaluated at $x = 1$ and was computed when this list was fixed, as were (E1)–(E5). Sol's caution, which a formal statement should respect: weakening the constraint need not enlarge the interval for every triple, because the other constraints can make it redundant (for the application's inputs the printed and the corrected systems give the same intervals); the claim is non-equivalence, shown by this witness, not that the printed system is wider everywhere. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1 with the full-compliance case $P_c = 1$ supplied, and the substitution in the proof of Corollary 1 written without a non-complier mean, as repaired by Sol
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), proof of Proposition 1 (‘Define $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$’ and ‘Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$’); p. 679 (PDF p. 3), proof of Corollary 1
canonical_claim.statement:
Sol's repair (validated.json, P028-E002, smallest_repair), verbatim: "Prepend to Proposition 1's proof: 'If P_c=1, every unit is a complier, so EY_c(0)=EY_0 and EY_c(1)=EY_1; the displayed intervals reduce to these singletons. Henceforth suppose 0<P_c<1.' If Corollary 1 is also to cover empty treatment-assignment cells, replace pure-cell probability-times-mean terms by m=E[Y·D|Z=0]+E[Y·(1-D)|Z=1] and use EY_c(z)=(EY_z-m)/P_c, avoiding a noncomplier mean."
Mathematical content, with every hypothesis (validator's derivation.md, sections 1 and 3–5). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$. Write $C$, $A$, $N$ for the compliers, always-takers and never-takers, $p = P_c = \Pr(C)$, $e_z = EY_z$ and $c_d = \mathrm{E}[Y(d)|C]$.
(i) [The assumptions allow the boundary.] $0 < p \le 1$, so $c_0$ and $c_1$ are defined; the assumptions do not imply $p < 1$ (P028-T7).
(ii) [Mixture equations with no mean over a possibly empty group.] Define the non-complier contribution $m = \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{1}_A\,Y(1)] + \mathrm{E}[\mathbf{1}_N\,Y(0)]$. Then $$0 \le m \le 1 - p, \qquad e_0 = p\,c_0 + m, \qquad e_1 = p\,c_1 + m.$$
(iii) [$m$ in observable terms.] $m = \mathrm{E}[Y \cdot D \mid Z = 0] + \mathrm{E}[Y \cdot (1 - D) \mid Z = 1]$, where $Y$ is the observed outcome and the products are ordinary multiplication.
(iv) [The two cases.] If $p < 1$, then $\Pr[D(1) = D(0)] = 1 - p > 0$, $EY_n = \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$ is defined, $m = (1 - p)\,EY_n$ with $0 \le EY_n \le 1$, and (ii) is Eqs. (1)–(2) of the printed proof. If $p = 1$, then $m = 0$, $c_0 = e_0$ and $c_1 = e_1$.
(v) [Corollary 1 without a non-complier mean; an optional extension to empty cells.] For every $p \in (0, 1]$, $c_0 = (e_0 - m)/p$ and $c_1 = (e_1 - m)/p$ with $m$ as in (iii); no cell $(D = d, Z = z)$ is required to have positive probability. When $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] > 0$ and $\Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] > 0$, $m = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$, and this is the formula printed in Corollary 1; the product moment of an empty cell is 0.
(vi) [The bounds for every $p \in (0, 1]$, with no division by $1 - p$.] Put $\tau = (e_1 - e_0)/p$. From (ii) and $0 \le c_0 \le 1$, $0 \le c_1 \le 1$: $c_1 = c_0 + \tau$; $0 \le e_1 - p\,c_1 \le 1 - p$, that is, $1 - (1 - e_1)/p \le c_1 \le e_1/p$; and $0 \le e_0 - p\,c_0 \le 1 - p$, that is, $1 - (1 - e_0)/p \le c_0 \le e_0/p$. Hence $c_0$ and $c_1$ lie in the two intervals of Proposition 1.
(vii) [The printed intervals at the boundary.] For all real $e_0, e_1 \in [0, 1]$, at $P_c = 1$ the intervals of Proposition 1 are the singletons $\{e_0\}$ and $\{e_1\}$: $$\max\{0,\ e_0 - e_1,\ e_0\} = \min\{1,\ 1 - e_1 + e_0,\ e_0\} = e_0, \qquad \max\{0,\ e_1 - e_0,\ e_1\} = \min\{1,\ 1 + e_1 - e_0,\ e_1\} = e_1.$$

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proof of Proposition 1, ‘Define $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$’ and ‘Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$’, used without the condition $P_c < 1$; the witness is the validator's and is not in the paper
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), proof of Proposition 1; the assumptions are in Section 2 on the same page; the related ratio is in the proof of Corollary 1, p. 679 (PDF p. 3)
canonical_claim.statement:
Exact witness (validator's; not in the paper): a model that satisfies every assumption of Section 2 and in which the non-complier group is empty, so that the proof's definition of $EY_n$ conditions on a null event and its division is by $1 - P_c = 0$.
The probability space has two atoms, each of probability $\tfrac12$. Atom 1: $Z = 0$, $D(0) = 0$, $D(1) = 1$, $Y(0) = 0$, $Y(1) = 1$; observed $D = 0$, $Y = 0$. Atom 2: $Z = 1$, $D(0) = 0$, $D(1) = 1$, $Y(0) = 0$, $Y(1) = 1$; observed $D = 1$, $Y = 1$. Here $Y(d, z) = Y(d)$, $D = D(Z)$ and $Y = Y(D)$.
Claims. (F1) The assumptions hold: $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ is constant, hence independent of $Z$; exclusion holds by the definition of $Y(d,z)$; $D(1) = 1 \ge 0 = D(0)$; $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = 1 \ne 0$; $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0, 1]$; $\Pr[Z = 0] = \Pr[Z = 1] = \tfrac12 > 0$. (F2) $P_c = 1$, $EY_0 = 0$, $EY_1 = 1$, $EY_c(0) = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = 0$ and $EY_c(1) = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = 1$. (F3) $\Pr[D(1) = D(0)] = 0$, $1 - P_c = 0$ and $EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = 0$: the conditioning event of $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$ has probability zero, and the printed quotient $[EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$ has numerator 0 and denominator 0. (F4) With $P_c = 1$, Eqs. (1) and (2) read $EY_c(0) = EY_0$ and $EY_c(1) = EY_1$ and hold for every real number put in the place of $EY_n$; so Eq. (2) does not determine $EY_n$, and the step ‘Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$’ is not available. (F5) $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 0$: the cells $(D = 1, Z = 0)$ and $(D = 0, Z = 1)$ are empty, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0]$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$ are conditional means on null events, and the ratio in the proof of Corollary 1 has denominator $\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1] = 0$ and, whatever values are assigned to the two empty-cell means (for instance $\tfrac13$ and $\tfrac23$), numerator 0. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Proposition 1, with its printed proof, Eqs. (1)–(3)
canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] The proposition is stated under the setting of Section 2: assumptions (i) random assignment, (ii) exclusion restriction, (iii) non-zero first-stage effect, (iv) monotonicity, the definitions $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$, and ‘we require that outcomes are bounded. Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$’ (transcribed in full in the standing assumptions).
[Sentence introducing it, Section 3, p. 678] “Proposition 1 asserts the intervals for complier potential outcomes identified under incomplete reporting.”
[p. 678] Proposition 1. When only $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $P_c$ are known, sharp bounds exist for the complier average potential outcomes. The average control potential outcome for compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ lies in $$\left[\max\left\{0,\ -\frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ 1 - \frac{1 - EY_0}{P_c}\right\},\ \min\left\{1,\ 1 - \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ \frac{EY_0}{P_c}\right\}\right].$$ Similarly, the average treated potential outcome for compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$, lies in $$\left[\max\left\{0,\ \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ 1 - \frac{1 - EY_1}{P_c}\right\},\ \min\left\{1,\ 1 + \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},\ \frac{EY_1}{P_c}\right\}\right].$$
[Proof as printed, p. 678] Proof. Define $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, $EY_c(0) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ and $EY_c(1) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$. By the law of total probability, $$P_c EY_c(0) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_0, \qquad (1)$$ $$P_c EY_c(1) + (1 - P_c)EY_n = EY_1, \qquad (2)$$ given the constraints that $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, and $0 \le EY_n \le 1$. Since $EY_n = [EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1)]/(1 - P_c)$, we may reframe the problem as $$P_c EY_c(0) + EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) = EY_0, \qquad (3)$$ such that $0 \le EY_c(0) \le 1$, $0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1$, and $0 \le EY_1 - P_c EY_c(1) \le 1$. Then substituting the implied value of $EY_c(1)$ from Eq. (3) into the system of inequalities and rearranging terms, we obtain $$0 \le EY_c(1) \le 1,$$ $$(EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le 1 + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c,$$ $$(EY_1 + P_c - 1)/P_c \le EY_c(1) \le EY_1/P_c,$$ which yields the interval for $EY_c(1)$ asserted by the proposition. The interval for $EY_c(0)$ follows via substitution from the equality in Eq. (3). $\square$
[The hypotheses printed are the setting of Section 2. No condition $P_c < 1$ is printed. The sentence after Eq. (3) is transcribed as printed, with the upper limit 1 and ‘the implied value of $EY_c(1)$’; its corrected form is P028-T4.]

[Bounded outcomes: Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678] ‘Without loss of generality, fix $Y \in [0, 1]$.’ [$EY_n$, $EY_c(0)$, $EY_c(1)$: first line of the printed proof, p. 678] $EY_n \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, $EY_c(0) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_c(1) \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)]$. canonical_claim.note: An exact population statement, so priority 3. The audit's formal reading (both fresh readers and the validators agree on it; it is not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$. Write $p = P_c$, $e_z = EY_z$, $\tau = (e_1 - e_0)/p$, $c_d = \mathrm{E}[Y(d)|D(1) > D(0)]$, and let $[L_0, U_0]$, $[L_1, U_1]$ be the two printed intervals. Validity: in every such model $L_0 \le c_0 \le U_0$ and $L_1 \le c_1 \le U_1$; moreover $c_1 = c_0 + \tau$, $L_1 = L_0 + \tau$ and $U_1 = U_0 + \tau$. Sharpness (‘when only $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $P_c$ are known’): for all real $p \in (0, 1]$ and $e_0, e_1 \in [0, 1]$ with $|e_1 - e_0| \le p$, and every $x_1 \in [L_1, U_1]$, there is a model satisfying the setting with $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (p, e_0, e_1)$, $c_1 = x_1$ and $c_0 = x_1 - \tau$; so every point of each interval, endpoints included, is attained, and no narrower interval is valid. The triples with $|e_1 - e_0| \le p$ are exactly those that arise from some model and exactly those for which the printed intervals are nonempty (the re-run of P028-E002 obtains the equivalent condition $\max\{0, e_0 - p, e_1 - p\} \le m \le \min\{1 - p, e_0, e_1\}$ on the non-complier contribution; the equivalence was checked when this list was fixed). Attaining models (validators' construction): if $p < 1$, a fraction $p$ of compliers with constant potential outcomes $(x_1 - \tau, x_1)$ and a fraction $1 - p$ of never-takers with both potential outcomes equal to $(e_1 - p\,x_1)/(1 - p)$, with $Z$ an independent fair coin; if $p = 1$, compliers only, with constant potential outcomes $(e_0, e_1)$. The proposition does not fix the split of non-compliers into always-takers and never-takers, so a model with never-takers only is permitted. The printed proof gives the validity half; the attainability half is left implicit, and its sentence after Eq. (3) and its treatment of $P_c = 1$ are the subjects of findings P028-E001 and P028-E002 (both Minor): the corrected steps are P028-T4 and P028-T6 and the counterexamples to the printed steps are P028-T5 and P028-T7. Neither finding changes the statement: both validators established that the two intervals are correct and sharp for every $P_c \in (0, 1]$. A complete derivation with no division by $1 - P_c$ is sections 3–4 of the artifact named here; the batch validator's derivation for $0 < P_c < 1$ is the docstring of validate/_batch/P028-B01/work/check_math.py. ‘Without loss of generality’ for $Y \in [0, 1]$ is a normalization of a bounded outcome; for the formal statement boundedness of both potential outcomes in $[0, 1]$ is an assumption. The unit index and the phrase ‘labels are exchangeable’ are the subject of P028-N002 (a clarity note): the generic-unit reading above needs no added assumption. Worked instances, recomputed in exact arithmetic when this list was fixed: the application's inputs $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1) = (21/100, 45/100, 51/100)$ give $[0, 5/7]$ and $[2/7, 1]$ (printed $[0, 0.71]$ and $[0.29, 1]$, p. 679); $(3/5, 83/300, 173/300)$ gives $[0, 83/180]$ and $[1/2, 173/180]$; $(1/2, 3/4, 3/4)$ gives $[1/2, 1]$ twice; $(1, e_0, e_1)$ gives $\{e_0\}$ and $\{e_1\}$. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up, with the caveats about the proof recorded above.

canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] The corollary is stated under the setting of Section 2: assumptions (i)–(iv) and the definitions of $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$ (transcribed in full in the standing assumptions).
[Sentence introducing it, p. 678] “For contrast, we state sufficient conditions for point identification in Corollary 1, following the well-known result in, e.g., Imbens and Rubin (1997).”
[p. 678] Corollary 1. If $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$, for $d, z \in \{0, 1\}$, are known, the complier average potential outcomes are point identified. $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$ is equal to $$\frac{EY_0 - \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] - \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]}{P_c}$$ and $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c$.
[Proof as printed, p. 679 (PDF p. 3)] Proof. The average outcome for non-compliers, $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]\,\mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]}{\Pr[D = 1|Z = 0] + \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]}.$$ Substitution of $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)]$ into Eqs. (1) and (2) yields the result. $\square$
[The hypotheses printed are the setting of Section 2 and the premise that $\mathrm{E}[Y|D = d, Z = z]$ and $\Pr[D = d|Z = z]$ are known for $d, z \in \{0, 1\}$. Eqs. (1) and (2) are those of the proof of Proposition 1, transcribed in P028-T8.]

canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity, so priority 3. The audit's formal reading (section 5 of the artifact named here; not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$, except that bounded outcomes are not needed (integrable potential outcomes suffice). Write $q = \Pr[D = 1|Z = 0]$, $r = \Pr[D = 0|Z = 1]$, $\mu_{10} = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 1, Z = 0]$, $\mu_{01} = \mathrm{E}[Y|D = 0, Z = 1]$. Premise on the ordinary reading: the four cell means exist, that is, every cell $(D = d, Z = z)$ has positive probability; given the setting this is $q > 0$ and $r > 0$ (two-sided noncompliance), which forces $P_c < 1$. Conclusions: (a) $q = \Pr(A)$, $r = \Pr(N)$ and $P_c = 1 - q - r$, where $A$ and $N$ are the always-takers and never-takers; (b) $\mu_{10} = \mathrm{E}[Y(1)|A]$ and $\mu_{01} = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|N]$; (c) the proof's display: $\mathrm{E}[Y|D(1) = D(0)] = (q\,\mu_{10} + r\,\mu_{01})/(q + r)$; (d) $\mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = (EY_0 - q\,\mu_{10} - r\,\mu_{01})/P_c$; (e) $\mathrm{E}[Y(1)|D(1) > D(0)] = \mathrm{E}[Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] + (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c = (EY_1 - q\,\mu_{10} - r\,\mu_{01})/P_c$. Finding P028-E002 (Minor) touches the proof, not the statement: the validator confirmed that the ratio in (c) cannot be carried to models with an empty cell (its denominator $q + r = 1 - P_c$ vanishes at full compliance, P028-T7), and found the corollary valid under its premise; the product-moment form that needs no positivity of cells is P028-T6 (v), an optional extension. Under one-sided noncompliance (exactly one of $q$, $r$ zero) the premise fails on the ordinary reading; the Opus fresh reader reports the formula exact on 4000 random models including one-sided cases and $P_c = 1$ when terms with zero probability are read as 0, which is the content of P028-T6 (v). The citation ‘Imbens and Rubin (1997)’ is the subject of P028-E003 (a volume number in the reference list; not a target). The application of this formula to incompletely recorded outcomes in Section 4 is the subject of P028-N005 (P028-T1 to P028-T3) and does not touch the corollary as a statement about the full joint law. Both fresh readers report that the claim held up (one with the empty-cell caveat).

canonical_claim.name_in_paper: The ‘LATE theorem’ display of Section 2 (unnumbered), with the Introduction's statement that the three reported figures do not identify the average potential outcomes for compliers
canonical_claim.location: p. 678 (PDF p. 2), Section 2, second paragraph; p. 677 (PDF p. 1), Section 1, first paragraph
canonical_claim.statement:
[Setting, Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] “We follow the setup of Angrist and Pischke (2009, Chapter 4). Let $Y_i(d, z)$ be the potential outcome of unit $i$ under treatment $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$, let $D_i(z)$ be the potential treatment of unit $i$ under assignment $z$, and let $Z_i$ be the treatment assigned to unit $i$. The causal effect for unit $i$ is then $Y_i(1, Z_i) - Y_i(0, Z_i)$. We assume (i) random assignment: $[Y_i(d, z), D_i(z) : d, z \in \{0, 1\}] \perp\!\!\!\perp Z_i$; (ii) exclusion restriction: $Y_i(d, z)$ does not depend on $z$, so we may write $Y_i(d, z) = Y_i(d)$; (iii) non-zero first-stage effect: $E[D_i(1) - D_i(0)] \ne 0$; (iv) monotonicity: $\forall i$, $D_i(1) \ge D_i(0)$. We make two notational simplifications. First, given (i), labels are exchangeable and so we drop notational dependence on $i$. Second, we define $P_c \equiv \Pr[D(1) > D(0)]$, $EY_1 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1]$, and $EY_0 \equiv \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]$.”
[Section 2, second paragraph, p. 678] “This setting implies that the ``LATE theorem'' (Angrist and Pischke, 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) holds: the CACE, $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$, is equal to $$\frac{\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0]}{\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0]} = \frac{EY_1 - EY_0}{P_c},$$ where each component may be estimated using sample analogues to population quantities.”
[Section 1, first paragraph, p. 677 (PDF p. 1)] “When reporting results from experiments with noncompliance, including encouragement designs, researchers often include estimates of the average outcomes in treatment, average outcomes in control and the difference in average take-up between assignment statuses. These figures are sufficient for estimating a complier average causal effect (CACE), sometimes referred to as a local average treatment effect (Angrist et al., 1996). Although sufficient information is typically estimable from the data (Imbens and Rubin, 1997), these three figures alone do not provide enough information to identify the average potential outcomes for compliers.”
[The hypotheses printed for the display are the setting of Section 2, assumptions (i)–(iv). The bounded-outcome assumption is introduced after the display and is not attached to it.]
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: [$Y(d)$, $D(z)$, $Z$, assumptions (i)–(iv), $P_c$, $EY_1$, $EY_0$: Section 2, first paragraph, p. 678 (PDF p. 2)] as transcribed in the statement. [CACE] ‘complier average causal effect (CACE), sometimes referred to as a local average treatment effect’ (Section 1, p. 677); in Section 2 it is $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$. [$\mathrm{E}[D|Z = z]$] the mean of the observed treatment given assignment; the observed $D$ and $Y$ are not defined in the paper ($D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$ on the validators' reading). [‘These three figures’] the average outcomes of units assigned to treatment and to control and the difference in average take-up between assignment statuses (Section 1, p. 677; abstract, p. 677), that is, $EY_1$, $EY_0$ and $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0] = P_c$. [‘Identify’] not defined in the paper. The cited theorem (Angrist and Pischke 2009, Theorem 4.4.1) is not staged and is not needed: the display follows from the setting.
canonical_claim.note: An exact population identity and a non-identification statement, so priority 3. No finding rated as an error concerns it; P028-N002 (the sentence on exchangeable labels) is a clarity note and the generic-unit reading needs no added assumption. The audit's formal reading (not printed in this form). Setting: one probability space (a generic unit) carrying $Z \in \{0,1\}$ with $0 < \Pr[Z = 1] < 1$, potential treatments $D(0), D(1) \in \{0,1\}$ and potential outcomes $Y(0), Y(1) \in [0,1]$ (exclusion is built in: $Y(d,z) = Y(d)$), with $(Y(0), Y(1), D(0), D(1))$ independent of $Z$, $D(1) \ge D(0)$, $\mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] \ne 0$, and observed $D = D(Z)$, $Y = Y(D(Z))$, except that bounded outcomes are not needed (integrable potential outcomes suffice). (a) First stage: $\mathrm{E}[D|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[D|Z = 0] = \mathrm{E}[D(1) - D(0)] = \Pr[D(1) > D(0)] = P_c$, and $P_c > 0$. (b) Reduced form: $\mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 1] - \mathrm{E}[Y|Z = 0] = P_c \cdot \mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)]$. (c) Hence the display: $\mathrm{E}[Y(1) - Y(0)|D(1) > D(0)] = (EY_1 - EY_0)/P_c$, with a nonzero denominator. (a) is section 1 of the artifact named here and (b) is the difference of the two mixture equations $e_z = p\,c_z + m$ of its section 3 (P028-T6 (ii)); both fresh readers verified the identity independently. (d) Non-identification of the levels: there are two models satisfying the setting with bounded outcomes that have the same $(P_c, EY_0, EY_1)$ and different complier means. Exact witness (the Sol fresh reader's check of this claim, built with the validators' attaining construction of P028-T8, and recomputed when this list was fixed): for each $t \in [\tfrac12, 1]$ take a fraction $\tfrac12$ of compliers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = t$ and a fraction $\tfrac12$ of never-takers with $Y(0) = Y(1) = \tfrac32 - t$, with $Z$ an independent fair coin; then $P_c = \tfrac12$, $EY_0 = EY_1 = \tfrac34$ and the CACE is 0 for every $t$, while both complier means equal $t$. The models $t = \tfrac12$ and $t = 1$ are such a pair. The paper's ‘do not provide enough information to identify’ is a general statement: at some triples the levels are identified (at $P_c = 1$, P028-T6 (vii); more generally whenever the intervals of Proposition 1 are single points), so the formal statement is existential, as in (d), and not ‘for every triple’. The estimation clause (‘may be estimated using sample analogues’, ‘logically equivalent to the Wald instrumental variables estimator’) is not part of the target.
